Catalytic Asymmetric Synthesis of Chiral Allenylic Fluorides Enabled
by Multiple Radical Sorting
Yingying Li, Xian Gong, Ye Yuan, Yuyang Bai, Huan Li, and Lingling Chu*
Abstract: Here, we disclose a nickel-catalyzed, three-
component asymmetric radical sorting strategy that
enables the enantioselective synthesis of axially chiral
allenylic ﬂuorides from readily available 1,3-enynes, ﬂuo-
roiodomethane, and alkyl bromides. This radical protocol
proceeds under mild, reductive conditions, accommo-
dates a broad range of functional groups, including those
found in complex bioactive molecules, and demonstrates
high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. A previously
unrecognized ﬂuorine effect proved essential in dictating
both reactivity and stereocontrol in this multicomponent
radical coupling. This discovery establishes an efﬁcient
protocol for enantioselective multiple radical sorting and
provides a modular platform for the catalytic synthesis of
ﬂuorine-containing axial chirality.
The design of efﬁcient synthetic methods to access struc-
turally diverse allenes continues to be a topic of great
signiﬁcance in modern organic chemistry, owing to their
broad utility in pharmaceuticals and advanced materials. [1–3]
As unique π -systems featuring orthogonal reactivity, allenes
also serve as versatile synthetic intermediates amenable to
a wide range of transformations. [4–8] Among them, axially
chiral allenes have attracted particular interest due to their
prevalence in natural products and their potential as chiral
ligands or bioactive compounds. [9–11] However, the selective
construction of such motifs—especially those bearing func-
tional handles for further elaboration—remains a formidable
synthetic challenge. [12–20] Within this context, axially chiral
ﬂuorine-containing allenes, [21,22] such as allenylic ﬂuorides,
represent an especially intriguing yet underexplored subclass.
Despite the rich chemistry of chiral allylic and propargylic
ﬂuorides[23–26] and the rising importance of ﬂuorinated motifs
in medicinal and materials chemistry, [27,28] general, and
enantioselective methods for synthesizing allenylic ﬂuorides
are conspicuously lacking (Figure 1i). T o date, only a racemic

In recent years, radical-based strategies for the asymmet-
ric construction of chiral allenes have garnered increasing
attention due to their ability to access reactivity modes com-
plementary to traditional closed-shell processes. [12–20] Central
to these methods are allenyl radicals—key intermediates
that can be readily generated through diverse pathways
and harnessed for C–C bond formation. [30–32] Among these
approaches, radical addition to 1,3-enynes has emerged
as particularly attractive, owing to the high reactivity of
the enyne motifs, their broad structural tunability, and
the accessibility of various radical precursors. [33] Despite
these advances, the asymmetric radical difunctionalization
of enynes remains largely underdeveloped (Figure 1ii).[19]
Existing examples have primarily relied on radical coupling
with cyanides, terminal alkynes, or aryl halides. [34–40] To
date, attempts involving alkyl halides have only afforded
racemic products with limited generality. [41] Expanding the
pool of viable radical coupling partners—especially those
that enable both structural diversity and enantiocontrol—
is essential for broadening access to axially chiral allene
frameworks, including those bearing medicinally relevant
functional groups.
The monoﬂuoromethyl (CH 2F) group has emerged as a
valuable bioisostere for hydroxymethyl and methyl groups,
offering unique physicochemical properties with minimal
steric impact. [42] Despite their growing importance, efﬁ-
cient catalytic strategies for the direct incorporation of
CH2F moieties into complex molecular scaffolds remain
underdeveloped.[43–46] This challenge stems largely from the
intrinsic instability of CH 2F anions and the high reactivity of
metal–CH2F species, which often undergo decomposition or
non-productive side reactions. [47–49] In contrast to the more
established protocols for asymmetric diﬂuoromethylation and
triﬂuoromethylation,[50,51] enantioselective methods for CH2F
incorporation are still in their infancy. [52]
Inspired by our ongoing efforts in asymmetric radical
cross-couplings,[53–60] we envisioned a nickel-catalyzed asym-
metric multiple-radical sorting strategy [61–65] for enabling
an unprecedented enantioselective synthesis of axially chi-
ral allenylic ﬂuorides from 1,3-enynes (Figure 1iii). We
hypothesized that ﬂuoroiodomethane (ICH 2F), a stable and
readily available reagent, could serve as a source of CH 2F
radicals through halogen atom transfer (XAT) or single-
electron transfer (SET) pathways. [66–69] When paired with
a chiral nickel catalyst and a second carbon-based radical

precursor, this design could forge the target products in
a single operation through an orchestrated radical sorting
sequence. Implementing this design requires overcoming
several signiﬁcant challenges. First, the concurrent genera-
tion and selective engagement of multiple carbon-centered
radicals—including CH 2F , alkyl, propargyl, and allenyl rad-
ical species—demands stringent control to avoid competing
pathways such as hydrogen atom transfer, homocoupling, or
two-component cross-couplings.[70] Second, achieving stereo-
control in reactions involving highly reactive allenyl radicals
and ﬂuoromethyl radicals remains particularly difﬁcult, espe-
cially in the context of axial chirality. [71] Third, the risk of
forming unstable α-ﬂuoro carbenoids from CH 2F precursors
necessitates careful tuning of the reaction conditions to
prevent decomposition.[47–49] Herein, we report the successful
realization of this strategy: a nickel-catalyzed, enantioselec-
tive three-component radical dialkylation of enynes with
ICH2F and alkyl bromides under mild reductive conditions
(Figure 1iii). This transformation enables the direct and
modular synthesis of axially chiral allenylic ﬂuorides with
excellent chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Notably, a
distinct ﬂuorine effect was uncovered, which proved critical
in governing both the reactivity and stereocontrol of this
multicomponent process.
We initiated our investigation by selecting 1,3-enyne 1 and
ﬂuoroiodomethane 3 as model substrates to explore the feasi-
bility of an enantioselective three-component radical coupling
reaction (T able 1). T o differentiate between radical species,

Upon single-electron reduction, 2 generates an electrophilic
α-carbonyl radical that is sterically and electronically distinct
from the CH 2F radical and thus expected to engage with the
enyne more selectively. Extensive optimization of reaction
parameters led to the identiﬁcation of an effective catalytic
system comprising NiBr2·(PPh3)2, a chiral pyridine–oxazoline
(Py–Ox) ligand, and stoichiometric zinc powder as the reduc-
tant in DMAc. Under these conditions, the desired allenylic
ﬂuoride 4 was obtained in 37% yield and 64% enantiomeric
excess (entries 1–4), conﬁrming the viability of chemo-, regio-
, and enantio-selective dialkylation. Screening of alternative
ligand scaffolds revealed the unique importance of the Py–Ox
framework: phosphine–oxazoline (L1), bi-imidazole (L2), and
bi-oxazoline (L3) ligands were largely ineffective for enabling
multicomponent cross-couplings (entries 1–3). Modifying the
Py–Ox structure further improved selectivity. Ligand L5,
featuring a bulkier indane-derived oxazoline, yielded a similar
result but slightly enhanced enantioselectivity (entry 5).
Substitution of the pyridine moiety with a pyrimidine ring
(L6) signiﬁcantly improved both yield (58%) and ee (72%)
(entry 6), suggesting electronic effects on the heteroaryl
unit strongly inﬂuence catalytic performance. Systematic
tuning of the pyridine ring reinforced this trend. A CF 3-
substituted Py–Ox ligand ( L7) enhanced enantioselectivity
to 82%, whereas an OMe-substituted analogue ( L8)l e dt o
diminished yield and stereocontrol (entries 7–8). Notably,
introducing a CF 3 group at the C6-position ( L9) completely
suppressed reactivity, likely due to steric hindrance (entry 9),
while the C5-substituted CF 3 analogue (L10) was moderately
effective (entry 10). With the optimal ligand identiﬁed, we
next turned to solvent effects. A mixed DMAc–toluene
system (v/v = 3:17) provided signiﬁcant improvements in
both yield and enantioselectivity relative to DMAc alone
(entries 11–13). Further lowering the reaction temperature to
−10 °C boosted the enantiomeric excess to 91%, albeit with
a considerably decreased yield (entry 14). Considering the
instability of enynes, we modiﬁed the reagent stoichiometry
by employing tertiary alkyl bromide 2 as the limiting reagent.
This adjustment delivered product 4 in 87% yield and 91%

With optimized conditions in hand, we next examined the
scope of this asymmetric radical sorting process. As outlined
in Scheme 1, a wide array of substituted 1,3-enynes partic-
ipated smoothly in the three-component coupling with two
different alkyl halides, alkyl bromide 2 and ICH2F 3, affording
axially chiral allenylic ﬂuorides with high levels of chemo-,
regio-, and enantioselectivity ( 4–21, up to 92% ee). The reac-
tion exhibited broad functional group tolerance under mild
conditions, accommodating ethers ( 4), esters ( 5–8), amides
(9), alkyl chlorides ( 11), silyl ethers ( 12), internal oleﬁns ( 16),
thioethers (17), and lactams (19). A variety of heteroaromatic
motifs, including thiophenes ( 13), indoles ( 14), thiazoles ( 15),
and carbazoles ( 20), were also well-tolerated. Beyond alkyl-
substituted enynes, aryl-substituted analogs, including those
bearing electron-rich or deﬁcient substituents, proved equally
effective and furnished the desired products in good yields
and high ee ( 22–28, up to 95% ee). Notably, aryl bromides
remained intact under the reaction conditions, offering a
valuable orthogonal handle for downstream derivatization
(25). Moreover, a ferrocenyl-substituted enyne delivered the
corresponding allenylic ﬂuoride in 67% yield and 89% ee,
further demonstrating the method’s versatility (28).
T o highlight the synthetic potential of this protocol,
particularly in the context of late-stage functionalization,
we explored a series of enyne derivatives derived from
bioactive molecules and pharmaceuticals under the standard
conditions. As shown in Scheme 1, substrates derived from
ciproﬁbrate ( 29), oxaprozin ( 30), pterostilbene ( 31), isoxepac
(32), febuxostat ( 33), indomethacin ( 34), and vitamin E ( 35)
all underwent efﬁcient coupling with alkyl bromide 2 and
ICH2F 3, affording the corresponding axially chiral allenylic
ﬂuorides in high yields and excellent ee (up to 93% ee).
Finally, the scalability of this protocol was demonstrated
by performing the model reaction on a 3.0 mmol scale,
which furnished product 4 in a yield and enantiomeric
excess comparable to those of small-scale transformation
(Scheme 1).
We next sought to evaluate the generality of the alkyl
radical precursors (Scheme 2). As anticipated, a range
of tertiary α-halo carbonyl compounds, including both α-
bromo esters and α-bromo amides, proved to be competent
radical precursors, affording the desired axially chiral allene
products in good yields and with high ee ( 36–45,u pt o
92% ee). In addition to linear α-bromo carbonyl compounds,
sterically encumbered esters bearing cyclobutyl ( 38)o r
cyclohexyl ( 39) substituents were also well-tolerated, deliv-
ering the corresponding chiral allenes efﬁciently. Moreover,
gem-diﬂuoromethyl substituted alkyl halides, including 2-
bromo-2,2-diﬂuoromethyl esters, amides, and phosphonates,
underwent the multicomponent coupling reaction with high
efﬁciency (40–45). The absolute conﬁguration of product ( S)-
45, ee of which is 99% after recrystallization, was unambigu-
ously conﬁrmed by single-crystal X-ray crystallography, [72]
and the stereochemistry of the remaining products was
assigned by analogy. Encouragingly, secondary α-bromo
esters were also suitable coupling partners, delivering the
corresponding allenylic ﬂuorides in moderate yield and high
ee ( 46, 78% yield, 91% ee, 82% ee). In these cases, the
diastereomeric ratio was approximately 1:1, consistent with
a radical mechanism involving non-stereospeciﬁc formation
of α-carbonyl radicals ( 46). Notably, even primary α-bromo
carbonyl compounds participated effectively in the trans-
formation, furnishing 1,4-dialkylated products with excellent
enantioselectivities, albeit with slightly reduced yields ( 47–
48). These results are particularly striking given the subtle
steric differences between the CH 2F radical and 1-alkyl
radicals, highlighting the chemoselectivity of this radical
sorting protocol.
T o gain insight into the mechanism of this asymmetric
transformation, we conducted a series of preliminary mech-
anistic experiments (Scheme 3). The addition of 3 equivalents
of TEMPO to the model reaction completely suppressed the
formation of the desired allenylic ﬂuoride 4, instead yielding a
5% of CH2F-TEMPO adduct 49,[73] and a 12% of α-carbonyl–
TEMPO adduct 50 (Scheme 3a). These ﬁndings suggest the
generation of two distinct alkyl radicals in one system. Control
experiments further clariﬁed their origins: formation of the
CH2F radical required the presence of nickel, ligand, and
zinc, while the α-carbonyl radical could be generated by zinc
alone (Scheme 3a). These observations imply that a low-
valent nickel species is required to promote the generation
of the CH 2F radical from ICH 2F . T o probe whetherα-ﬂuoro
carbenoid intermediates might be involved, we carried out the
model reaction in the presence of 5 equivalents of D 2O, which
gave the desired product 4 in comparable yield and ee, with no
detectable formation of any α–CHDF or –CD2F products (see
Supporting Information for details). This result suggests that
a carbenoid mechanism is less likely involved. [74]
T o further examine the importance of ﬂuorine in reac-
tivity and selectivity, we substituted ICH 2Fw i t ho t h e r
α-haloalkanes (Scheme 3b). Use of ICH 2Cl or ICH 2Br under
standard conditions resulted in complex mixtures with no
observable dialkylation products (entries 1–3), likely due to
the propensity of these substrates to generate free carbenes
in the presence of zinc. While replacing ICH 2Fw i t hI C H3
led to no observable methylation product, and most of the
starting material remained untouched (entry 4), underscoring
the unique role of the ﬂuorine atom in facilitating the requisite
multiple radical sorting. Beyond the slightly higher reactivity
of ICH2F relative to ICH 3, we propose that polarity matching
between radical intermediates is central to both the reactivity
and selectivity observed in this transformation (Scheme 3b).
Mechanistically, four radical species are implicated: the α-
carbonyl radical ( ω = 1.38 eV), which adds to the enyne to
form an alkynyl radical (ω = 1.15 eV) that rapidly equilibrates
with its allenyl radical isomer ( ω ≈ 1.08 eV). [75] In the ﬁnal
step, nickel-mediated radical–radical coupling proceeds more
efﬁciently with the moderately nucleophilic CH 2F radical
(ω = 1.08 eV) than with the electronically neutral methyl
radical ( ω = 1.21 eV), thereby enabling the exceptional
chemo- and enantioselectivity of this radical sorting protocol.

Based on our mechanistic studies, we propose a plausible
catalytic cycle for this asymmetric radical sorting reaction
(Figure 2). Reduction of the Ni(II) precatalyst with zinc
generates Ni(I) complex I, which then undergoes a single-
electron transfer or a halogen atom abstraction with ICH 2F,
producing an α-ﬂuoroalkyl radical II and a Ni(II) intermedi-
ate III. A radical recombination between II and III furnishes
a( C H2F)Ni(III) complex IV, which is then reduced by zinc
to generate the key (CH 2F)Ni(II) species V. In parallel,
the α-bromo carbonyl compound VI undergoes a single-
electron reduction—either by zinc or by a low-valent nickel
species—to yield the electrophilic α-carbonyl radical VII.T h i s
radical then undergoes regioselective addition to enyne VIII,
generating the alkynyl radical IX, which rapidly equilibrates

In summary, we have developed an asymmetric multiple-
radical sorting strategy that enables the enantioselective
synthesis of axially chiral allenylic ﬂuorides from 1,3-enynes,
ICH2F , and alkyl bromides via nickel catalysis. This mild,
reductive protocol operates without organometallic reagents
and accommodates a wide range of enynes and aliphatic
electrophiles, delivering α-CH2F–substituted chiral allenes
with excellent chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Mecha-
nistic studies reveal a pathway involving two C(sp 3) radicals
and an allenyl radical, selectively orchestrated by a chiral
nickel complex, and highlight the unique role of ﬂuorine
in modulating both reactivity and stereocontrol. This work
establishes a versatile platform for constructing ﬂuorine-
containing axial chirality with high efﬁciency and broad
synthetic utility.

Catalytic Asymmetric Synthesis of Chiral Allenylic Fluorides Enabled
by Multiple Radical Sorting
Yingying Li, Xian Gong, Ye Yuan, Yuyang Bai, Huan Li, and Lingling Chu*

Abstract: Here, we disclose a nickel-catalyzed, three-
component asymmetric radical sorting strategy that
enables the enantioselective synthesis of axially chiral
allenylic fluorides from readily available 1,3-enynes, fluo-
roiodomethane, and alkyl bromides. This radical protocol
proceeds under mild, reductive conditions, accommo-
dates a broad range of functional groups, including those
found in complex bioactive molecules, and demonstrates
high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. A previously
unrecognized fluorine effect proved essential in dictating
both reactivity and stereocontrol in this multicomponent
radical coupling. This discovery establishes an efficient
protocol for enantioselective multiple radical sorting and
provides a modular platform for the catalytic synthesis of
fluorine-containing axial chirality.

The design of efficient synthetic methods to access struc-
turally diverse allenes continues to be a topic of great
significance in modern organic chemistry, owing to their
broad utility in pharmaceuticals and advanced materials.<sup>[1–3]</sup>
As unique π-systems featuring orthogonal reactivity, allenes
also serve as versatile synthetic intermediates amenable to
a wide range of transformations.<sup>[4–8]</sup> Among them, axially
chiral allenes have attracted particular interest due to their
prevalence in natural products and their potential as chiral
ligands or bioactive compounds.<sup>[9–11]</sup> However, the selective
construction of such motifs—especially those bearing func-
tional handles for further elaboration—remains a formidable
synthetic challenge.<sup>[12–20]</sup> Within this context, axially chiral
fluorine-containing allenes,<sup>[21,22]</sup> such as allenylic fluorides,
represent an especially intriguing yet underexplored subclass.
Despite the rich chemistry of chiral allylic and propargylic
fluorides<sup>[23–26]</sup> and the rising importance of fluorinated motifs
in medicinal and materials chemistry,<sup>[27,28]</sup> general, and
enantioselective methods for synthesizing allenylic fluorides
are conspicuously lacking (Figure 1i). To date, only a racemic

example of allenylic fluorides has been reported via radi-
cal fluorination,<sup>[29]</sup> highlighting the pressing need for new
strategies to access these valuable scaffolds.

In recent years, radical-based strategies for the asymmet-
ric construction of chiral allenes have garnered increasing
attention due to their ability to access reactivity modes com-
plementary to traditional closed-shell processes.<sup>[12–20]</sup> Central
to these methods are allenyl radicals—key intermediates
that can be readily generated through diverse pathways
and harnessed for C–C bond formation.<sup>[30–32]</sup> Among these
approaches, radical addition to 1,3-enynes has emerged
as particularly attractive, owing to the high reactivity of
the enyne motifs, their broad structural tunability, and
the accessibility of various radical precursors.<sup>[33]</sup> Despite
these advances, the asymmetric radical difunctionalization
of enynes remains largely underdeveloped (Figure 1ii).<sup>[19]</sup>
Existing examples have primarily relied on radical coupling
with cyanides, terminal alkynes, or aryl halides.<sup>[34–40]</sup> To
date, attempts involving alkyl halides have only afforded
racemic products with limited generality.<sup>[41]</sup> Expanding the
pool of viable radical coupling partners—especially those
that enable both structural diversity and enantiocontrol—
is essential for broadening access to axially chiral allene
frameworks, including those bearing medicinally relevant
functional groups.

The monofluoromethyl (CH F) group has emerged as a
valuable bioisostere for hydroxymethyl and methyl groups,
offering unique physicochemical properties with minimal
steric impact.<sup>[42]</sup> Despite their growing importance, effi-
cient catalytic strategies for the direct incorporation of
CH<sub>2</sub>F moieties into complex molecular scaffolds remain
underdeveloped.<sup>[43–46]</sup> This challenge stems largely from the
intrinsic instability of CH F anions and the high reactivity of
metal–CH F species, which often undergo decomposition or
non-productive side reactions.<sup>[47–49]</sup> In contrast to the more
established protocols for asymmetric difluoromethylation and
trifluoromethylation,<sup>[50,51]</sup> enantioselective methods for CH<sub>2</sub>F
incorporation are still in their infancy.<sup>[52]</sup>

Inspired by our ongoing efforts in asymmetric radical
cross-couplings,<sup>[53–60]</sup> we envisioned a nickel-catalyzed asym-
metric multiple-radical sorting strategy<sup>[61–65]</sup> for enabling
an unprecedented enantioselective synthesis of axially chi-
ral allenylic fluorides from 1,3-enynes (Figure 1iii). We
hypothesized that fluoroiodomethane (ICH F), a stable and
readily available reagent, could serve as a source of CH F
radicals through halogen atom transfer (XAT) or single-
electron transfer (SET) pathways.<sup>[66–69]</sup> When paired with
a chiral nickel catalyst and a second carbon-based radical

precursor, this design could forge the target products in
a single operation through an orchestrated radical sorting
sequence. Implementing this design requires overcoming
several significant challenges. First, the concurrent genera-
tion and selective engagement of multiple carbon-centered
radicals—including CH<sub>2</sub>F, alkyl, propargyl, and allenyl rad-
ical species—demands stringent control to avoid competing
pathways such as hydrogen atom transfer, homocoupling, or
two-component cross-couplings.<sup>[70]</sup> Second, achieving stereo-
control in reactions involving highly reactive allenyl radicals
and fluoromethyl radicals remains particularly difficult, espe-
cially in the context of axial chirality.<sup>[71]</sup> Third, the risk of
forming unstable α-fluoro carbenoids from CH<sub>2</sub>F precursors
necessitates careful tuning of the reaction conditions to

prevent decomposition.<sup>[47–49]</sup> Herein, we report the successful
realization of this strategy: a nickel-catalyzed, enantioselec-
tive three-component radical dialkylation of enynes with
ICH F and alkyl bromides under mild reductive conditions
(Figure 1iii). This transformation enables the direct and
modular synthesis of axially chiral allenylic fluorides with
excellent chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Notably, a
distinct fluorine effect was uncovered, which proved critical
in governing both the reactivity and stereocontrol of this
multicomponent process.

With optimized conditions in hand, we next examined the
scope of this asymmetric radical sorting process. As outlined
in Scheme 1, a wide array of substituted 1,3-enynes partic-

different alkyl halides, alkyl bromide 2 and ICH F 3, affording
axially chiral allenylic fluorides with high levels of chemo-,
regio-, and enantioselectivity (4–21, up to 92% ee). The reac-

conditions, accommodating ethers (4), esters (5–8), amides

and carbazoles (20), were also well-tolerated. Beyond alkyl-
substituted enynes, aryl-substituted analogs, including those
bearing electron-rich or deficient substituents, proved equally
effective and furnished the desired products in good yields
and high ee (22–28, up to 95% ee). Notably, aryl bromides
remained intact under the reaction conditions, offering a
valuable orthogonal handle for downstream derivatization
(25). Moreover, a ferrocenyl-substituted enyne delivered the
corresponding allenylic fluoride in 67% yield and 89% ee,
further demonstrating the method’s versatility (28).

To highlight the synthetic potential of this protocol,
particularly in the context of late-stage functionalization,
we explored a series of enyne derivatives derived from
bioactive molecules and pharmaceuticals under the standard
conditions. As shown in Scheme 1, substrates derived from
ciprofibrate (29), oxaprozin (30), pterostilbene (31), isoxepac
(32), febuxostat (33), indomethacin (34), and vitamin E (35)
all underwent efficient coupling with alkyl bromide 2 and
ICH F 3, affording the corresponding axially chiral allenylic
fluorides in high yields and excellent ee (up to 93% ee).
Finally, the scalability of this protocol was demonstrated
by performing the model reaction on a 3.0 mmol scale,
which furnished product 4 in a yield and enantiomeric
excess comparable to those of small-scale transformation
(Scheme 1).

of tertiary α-halo carbonyl compounds, including both α-

radical precursors, affording the desired axially chiral allene
products in good yields and with high ee (36–45, up to
92% ee). In addition to linear α-bromo carbonyl compounds,
sterically encumbered esters bearing cyclobutyl (38) or
cyclohexyl (39) substituents were also well-tolerated, deliv-
ering the corresponding chiral allenes efficiently. Moreover,
gem-difluoromethyl substituted alkyl halides, including 2-
bromo-2,2-difluoromethyl esters, amides, and phosphonates,
underwent the multicomponent coupling reaction with high
efficiency (40–45). The absolute configuration of product (S)-

and the stereochemistry of the remaining products was

assigned by analogy. Encouragingly, secondary α-bromo
esters were also suitable coupling partners, delivering the
corresponding allenylic fluorides in moderate yield and high

diastereomeric ratio was approximately 1:1, consistent with
a radical mechanism involving non-stereospecific formation
of α-carbonyl radicals (46). Notably, even primary α-bromo

formation, furnishing 1,4-dialkylated products with excellent
enantioselectivities, albeit with slightly reduced yields (47–
48). These results are particularly striking given the subtle
steric differences between the CH F radical and 1-alkyl
radicals, highlighting the chemoselectivity of this radical
sorting protocol.

Based on our mechanistic studies, we propose a plausible
catalytic cycle for this asymmetric radical sorting reaction
(Figure 2). Reduction of the Ni(II) precatalyst with zinc
generates Ni(I) complex I, which then undergoes a single-
electron transfer or a halogen atom abstraction with ICH F,
producing an α-fluoroalkyl radical II and a Ni(II) intermedi-
ate III. A radical recombination between II and III furnishes
a (CH F)Ni(III) complex IV, which is then reduced by zinc

electron reduction—either by zinc or by a low-valent nickel
species—to yield the electrophilic α-carbonyl radical VII. This
radical then undergoes regioselective addition to enyne VIII,
generating the alkynyl radical IX, which rapidly equilibrates

In summary, we have developed an asymmetric multiple-
radical sorting strategy that enables the enantioselective
synthesis of axially chiral allenylic fluorides from 1,3-enynes,
ICH F, and alkyl bromides via nickel catalysis. This mild,
reductive protocol operates without organometallic reagents
and accommodates a wide range of enynes and aliphatic
electrophiles, delivering

with excellent chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Mecha-

nickel complex, and highlight the unique role of fluorine
in modulating both reactivity and stereocontrol. This work
establishes a versatile platform for constructing fluorine-
containing axial chirality with high efficiency and broad
synthetic utility.
